guides.title: Configuring Ergosfare
guides.description: Registration entry points, the two ways to select from the frozen composition table, and the knobs on AddErgosfare.
guides.body:
Everything Ergosfare needs at runtime comes from one call:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(q => q.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(e => e.RegisterGenerated()));
```

`AddErgosfare` takes an `Action<IModuleRegistry>`. Each `AddXModule` call opens a module
builder that **selects** from the compiled composition table for this container. Only add the
modules you use — an application that never publishes events has no reason to register the
event module.

## Registration is selection

The source generator compiles the whole closure's handlers and interceptors into a frozen
composition table before the application runs. Registration does not discover anything; it
records which of that table's participant rows *this* container runs. Selection is a union,
so registering the same type twice — or through two different calls — is harmless.

A row nobody selected is not part of any pipeline, and a container that selected nothing runs
nothing. That is the whole failure model: a message with no selected handler raises
`NoHandlerFoundException`.

### Generated (preferred)

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
```

The bulk path. The generator names every command construct it discovered — in your
compilation *and in referenced assemblies* — and emits dispatch roots so Native AOT has a
static anchor for every generic instantiation. See
[Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery).

`RegisterGenerated("reporting.*")` narrows the same call to the constructs whose
[discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys) match a pattern.

### Explicit

```csharp
.AddCommandModule(c => c
    .Register<CreateProductHandler>()
    .Register(typeof(LogCommands)))
```

Useful when you want a construct selected under conditions the generator cannot see — a
feature flag read from configuration, for example. The type still has to exist in the
compiled table; `Register<T>()` chooses, it does not add.

{% aside type="caution" %}
There is no third way. `RegisterFromAssembly(...)`, `RegisterDescriptors(...)` and the
`IMessageRegistry` surface were removed in v2.3 — a dynamically loaded assembly cannot append
a message shape after compilation. See
[Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3).
{% /aside %}

## Handler lifetimes

Handlers and interceptors resolve from the **calling DI scope** on every dispatch. Their
lifetime is whatever you registered them as:

| Registration | Behaviour per dispatch |
|---|---|
| Singleton | Container-cached; one instance for the process |
| Scoped | One instance per DI scope |
| Transient | A new instance for every dispatch |

Transient handlers allocating once per dispatch is not a leak — it is what a transient
registration declares. For dispatch-heavy loops inside a single scope that want instance
reuse, either register handlers as singletons or opt in globally:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .ForceMemoizedHandlers()
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated()));
```

## Per-dispatch settings

Each module's mediator takes an optional settings object. It carries a group filter and a
seed for the context's item bag:

```csharp
var settings = new CommandMediationSettings
{
    Items = { ["tenant"] = tenantId }
};
settings.Filters.Groups = ["audit"];

await commands.SendAsync(new CreateProduct("Laptop", 999m), settings);
```

- **`Filters.Groups`** restricts the pipeline to handlers and interceptors carrying a
  matching `[Group]`. An empty collection means "everything registered". See
  [Groups and weights](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).
- **`Items`** seeds `context.Items` for this dispatch.

Group filters participate in the pipeline plan cache key, so the filtering itself is done once
per `(message type, group set)` rather than per dispatch. A filtered dispatch is still not free
relative to an unfiltered one: **generated plans are only consulted for a group-less dispatch**,
so filtering means taking the general executor path. Prefer
[`GroupSet`](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights#groupset--the-reusable-filter)
over a fresh settings object when you do filter.

## Result adapters

When a handler returns a value-carried failure — a foreign `Result<T>` type — an
`IResultAdapter<TResult>` surfaces that failure out of the pipeline without the handler
throwing. The binding is declarative, per message:

```csharp
[ResultAdapter(typeof(MyResultAdapter))]
public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : ICommand<MyResult<Guid>>;
```

The framework's own `Result` / `Result<T>` carriers need no annotation, and an unannotated
message with any other result type is not probed at all. `[IgnoreResultAdapter]` opts a
message out.

For a codebase-wide carrier, configure one fallback instead of annotating every message:

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(MyResultAdapter<>))
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated()));
```

The type may be closed over one result type or an open generic definition closed per served
result; it needs a public parameterless constructor, and a bad type fails inside
`AddErgosfare` rather than on some first dispatch.

{% aside type="caution" %}
This binding surface is `[Experimental]` under **`ERGOEXP001`** — `[ResultAdapter]`,
`[IgnoreResultAdapter]` and `UseDefaultResultAdapter` alike. The value channel's semantics
are settled; the way you bind to it may still shift in a minor release. See
[Experimental APIs](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/experimental-apis).
{% /aside %}

## What is *not* configurable

Two omissions are deliberate:

- **The execution context exposes no service provider.** Handler resolution belongs to the
  dispatcher. If a handler needs a service, take it in the constructor.
- **There is no ambient context.** `AmbientExecutionContext` was removed in v2. The context
  is a parameter on every handler and interceptor, and the only way to reach it. See
  [Execution context](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/execution-context).

Next: [Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery).

guides.title: Installation
guides.description: Which Ergosfare packages you need, and why the source generator is a separate one.
guides.body:
Ergosfare v2 is the stable line on nuget.org, so a plain `dotnet add package` gets it. If you
want the in-development line instead, the [preview docs](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/installation)
cover it.

## The short version

For an application:

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator
```

`Stella.Ergosfare` is a convenience bundle that pulls in the Commands, Queries and Events
modules with their DI extensions. `Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator` is what produces
`RegisterGenerated()`.

{% aside type="caution" %}
The source generator is a **separate package on purpose**, but it is not optional in
practice. It is what compiles the frozen composition table and emits `RegisterGenerated()`;
without it a container has nothing to select from and every dispatch fails with
`NoHandlerFoundException`. Runtime assembly scanning was removed in v2.3 — see
[Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3).
{% /aside %}

## Requirements

- **.NET 9.0, .NET 10.0 or .NET 11.0.** The libraries multi-target
  `net9.0;net10.0;net11.0`. The `net11.0` assets carry no extra API — they exist as proof the
  sources compile under the C# 15 compiler and hold the contract suite on .NET 11. A
  `net11.0` project without them already binds `lib/net10.0/` through roll-forward.
- **C# `latest`.** The generated registration code is deliberately conservative, but the
  abstractions use current language features.

{% aside type="note" %}
.NET 11 reaches GA on 2026-11-10. Until then the `net11.0` assets are compiled against
**preview reference packs** and will be re-packed against the GA pack once it ships. Targeting
`net9.0` or `net10.0` avoids the question entirely and loses nothing.
{% /aside %}

## Picking packages deliberately

The umbrella package is convenient, not required. Each module is independent:

| Package | What it gives you |
|---|---|
| `Stella.Ergosfare` | Umbrella — Commands + Queries + Events + DI extensions |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator` | Compile-time discovery, `RegisterGenerated()`, dispatch roots |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions` | `ErgosfareContext`, attributes, handler contracts |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions` | `ICommand`, `ICommandHandler`, command interceptors |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Queries.Abstractions` | `IQuery`, `IStreamQuery`, query handlers and interceptors |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Events.Abstractions` | `IEvent`, `IEventHandler`, event interceptors |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.Core` | Runtime: composition catalog, pipeline plans, dispatch |
| `Stella.Ergosfare.*.Extensions.MicrosoftDependencyInjection` | `AddErgosfare`, `AddCommandModule`, module builders |

### Library that only declares messages and handlers

Reference just the abstractions. This keeps the library free of the runtime and of any DI
container dependency:

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions
```

The library needs **no registration code**. When an application that references it runs the
source generator, the generator walks referenced assemblies and registers those handlers
through the application's own `RegisterGenerated()`. See
[Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery).

### Application that only uses commands

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.Commands
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Extensions.MicrosoftDependencyInjection
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator
```

## Verifying the generator is running

The generator writes a single file into your compilation. After a build you can find it at:

```
obj/gen/Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator/…/ErgosfareRegistrations.g.cs
```

Open it and you should see an `internal static class ErgosfareGeneratedRegistrations` in
namespace `Stella.Ergosfare.Generated`. If `RegisterGenerated()` does not resolve in your
startup code, the usual cause is a missing using:

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Generated;
```

## Reference scanning

By default the generator also inspects referenced assemblies so that handlers shipped by
libraries register automatically. To turn that off for a project:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>false</ErgosfareSourceGeneratorScanReferences>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Next: [Quick start](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/quick-start) wires up a command, a query
and an event in one file.

guides.title: Introduction
guides.description: Ergosfare is a source-generated, high-performance mediator for CQRS-style messaging in .NET — commands, queries and events over one pipeline model.
guides.body:
Ergosfare is a mediator for CQRS-style messaging in .NET: commands, queries and events over
one pipeline model. It is built around a single design premise — **all dispatch-shape work
happens at compile time or once per message type, never per dispatch**.

A Roslyn source generator compiles a **frozen composition table** — one immutable
composition per message type, holding its handler rows and its four interceptor stages in
execution order — and emits the registration that selects from it. Pipeline plans are
computed once per `(message type, group set)` and cached process-wide. Dispatch generics are
closed at compile time, and execution contexts are pooled. A dispatch resolves handler
*instances* from the calling DI scope and walks a pre-built plan — no reflection, no
`MakeGenericType`, no assembly scan, no `AsyncLocal`, and no per-dispatch context allocation
on the hot path.

{% aside %}
You are reading the docs for the **stable v2 line**, built from the
[`main` branch](https://github.com/stellayazilim/Ergosfare/tree/main). Work in progress lands
on the [preview line](/ergosfare.docs/preview/getting-started/introduction) first. Upgrading
from v2.2? v2.3 removed the runtime registry — see
[Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3). Coming from v1? See
[Migrating from v1](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v1-to-v2).
{% /aside %}

## What it looks like

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Commands.Abstractions;
using Stella.Ergosfare.Core.Abstractions;

public sealed record CreateProduct(string Name) : ICommand<Guid>;

public sealed class CreateProductHandler : ICommandHandler<CreateProduct, Guid>
{
    public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(Guid.NewGuid());
}
```

Nothing registers this handler by hand. The source generator finds it at compile time and
emits the registration call you wire up once at startup:

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Generated;

builder.Services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(q => q.RegisterGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(e => e.RegisterGenerated()));
```

## Why Ergosfare

**Compile-time registration.** The generator discovers handlers in your compilation *and in
referenced assemblies*, compiles their relationships into the frozen composition table, and
emits `RegisterGenerated()`. A library's handlers register through the consuming app's
generated code with no registration code in the library at all.

**Registration is selection, not discovery.** `RegisterGenerated()` and `Register<T>()` pick
which rows of the compiled table one container runs. Repeated and overlapping selections are
harmless unions, and nothing can append a message shape after compilation — so there is no
registration window whose timing changes a running application.

**Reflection-free dispatch.** Generated dispatch roots close executor generics at compile
time, and pipeline plans pre-close generic handler types. `MakeGenericType` survives only as
a fallback for message types the generator could not root, chiefly open generics.

**Allocation you can account for.** Pooled execution contexts, a `ValueTask`-first surface
and generated plans put a no-result command at 19.9 ns / 24 B and a result query at
24.0 ns / 24 B per dispatch. See [Performance](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/performance) for the
measured shapes and how to read them.

**Nested dispatch, safely.** `context.CreateScope()` gives a handler an isolated child
context with inherited cancellation for mediator calls inside handlers — the pattern
ambient-state mediators cannot offer safely.

**No ambient state.** The execution context is a parameter, never an `AsyncLocal`. Nothing
about a dispatch is discoverable from thread-local storage, which is what makes nested and
parallel dispatch predictable.

**Native AOT and trimming.** Every construct is referenced statically via `typeof`, and
dispatch roots anchor every generic instantiation — including `record struct` messages,
which shared generic code cannot cover.

**Modular.** Commands, Queries and Events are independent packages over a shared core.
A library that only declares messages needs just the relevant `.Abstractions` package.

## How a dispatch fits together

```
compile time                    once per (message type, groups)         every dispatch
────────────                    ───────────────────────────────         ──────────────
source generator         ──►    composition ─► selection ─► plan     ──►  pooled context rented
  frozen composition table        │                                          │
  dispatch roots emitted          │  six fixed stages, pre-ordered           │  executor closed over runtime type
  RegisterGenerated()             │  (direct-first, weight-ordered)          │  handler resolved from calling scope
                                  └─ closed generic types pre-computed       └─ pre → main → post/exception → final
```

- **Composition and selection.** The generator compiles one `FrozenComposition` per message
  type into a process-wide table. Registration selects which of its participant rows this
  container runs — `RegisterGenerated()` in bulk, `Register<T>()` one at a time. Selection is
  a union, so the two are safe to combine and repeat.
- **Pipeline plan.** Six fixed stages per message: main handlers (split direct/indirect) and
  four interceptor stages, each a pre-ordered array. Direct entries come first, then
  covariant matches ordered by weight. Group filters and `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` are applied
  here, once.
- **Dispatch.** The mediator rents a pooled context, looks up the cached executor for the
  message's runtime type, and walks the plan. Handler resolution belongs to the dispatcher —
  the execution context deliberately exposes **no** service provider.

## Where to go next

- [Installation](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/installation) — which packages you actually need.
- [Quick start](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/quick-start) — a command, a query and an event, end to end.
- [Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery) — where `RegisterGenerated()` comes from.
- [Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3) — what v2.3 removed, and the replacement for each.
- [Migrating from v1](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v1-to-v2) — if you are still on the v1 line.

{% aside type="note" %}
Stuck on something? Open an issue on
[GitHub](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/issues).
{% /aside %}

guides.title: Using Ergosfare docs with AI
guides.description: Connect the Ergosfare documentation to Codex, Claude, Cursor, VS Code, or any stdio-compatible MCP client.
guides.body:
Ergosfare publishes its guides and generated API reference as an
[MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/getting-started/intro) catalog. Connect it once and
your AI coding client can search the current documentation, read complete pages, and look up
exact public API names without cloning the docs repository or pasting pages into a prompt.

The MCP server runs locally through `npx` and reads the catalog from the public docs site. It
does not require an API key.

{% aside type="note" %}
You need a current [Node.js LTS](https://nodejs.org/) installation. Confirm that both Node.js
and npm are available with `node --version` and `npx --version`.
{% /aside %}

## Codex

Add the server from a terminal:

```bash
codex mcp add ergosfare-docs -- npx -y @stellayazilim/mcp-starlight https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs
```

Alternatively, add it to `~/.codex/config.toml` for all projects, or to
`.codex/config.toml` in a trusted project:

```toml
[mcp_servers.ergosfare-docs]
command = "npx"
args = ["-y", "@stellayazilim/mcp-starlight", "https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs"]
```

Run `codex mcp list` to verify the connection. Codex CLI, the Codex IDE extension, and the
ChatGPT desktop app use the same MCP configuration on the same host.

## Claude Desktop

Open **Settings → Developer → Edit Config**, then add this entry to
`claude_desktop_config.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ergosfare-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@stellayazilim/mcp-starlight", "https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Save the file and fully restart Claude Desktop. If the file already contains other servers,
merge `ergosfare-docs` into the existing `mcpServers` object instead of replacing it.

## Claude Code

Add the server for the current project with one command:

```bash
claude mcp add ergosfare-docs -- npx -y @stellayazilim/mcp-starlight https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs
```

To share the setup with your team, commit a `.mcp.json` file at the project root:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ergosfare-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@stellayazilim/mcp-starlight", "https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Run `claude mcp list` or use `/mcp` inside Claude Code to check its status. Project-scoped
servers require workspace approval when the repository is opened for the first time.

## Cursor

Add the following to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for all projects, or to `.cursor/mcp.json` in one
project:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "ergosfare-docs": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@stellayazilim/mcp-starlight", "https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Restart or reload Cursor after saving the file, then enable `ergosfare-docs` in the MCP
settings if it is not already active.

## VS Code and GitHub Copilot

Create `.vscode/mcp.json` in your project:

```json
{
  "servers": {
    "ergosfare-docs": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@stellayazilim/mcp-starlight", "https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs"]
    }
  }
}
```

Start the server from the inline action in `mcp.json`, or run **MCP: List Servers** from the
Command Palette. VS Code asks you to trust a new local server before starting it.

## Other MCP clients

Any MCP client that supports local stdio servers can use the same launch command:

```text
npx -y @stellayazilim/mcp-starlight https://stellayazilim.github.io/ergosfare.docs
```

Use `ergosfare-docs` as the server name and map the executable to `npx` and the remaining
tokens to its argument list. Configuration envelopes differ between clients: many use
`mcpServers`, while VS Code uses `servers`.

{% aside type="caution" %}
An stdio MCP server is a local process running with your user permissions. Review packages
before allowing `npx` to execute them, and review team-shared MCP configuration before you
approve a project.
{% /aside %}

## Ask useful questions

The integration exposes documentation search, full-page reading, page listing, and exact API
reference search. Tell the assistant which documentation line you want so stable and preview
APIs are not mixed.

Try prompts such as:

- “Using `ergosfare-docs`, show me the smallest stable command and handler setup.”
- “Search the preview docs for group-aware dispatch plans and explain the generated path.”
- “Find the exact public signature of `ICommandMediator.SendAsync` in the API reference.”
- “Compare the stable and preview guidance for compile-time discovery; cite the pages used.”
- “Read the Turkish quick start and adapt it to this project.”

The server checks for a newer published catalog while tools are being used, so a long-lived
client can pick up documentation deployments without reinstalling the package.

## Troubleshooting

- If the server does not start, verify `node`, `npm`, and `npx` are available to the client,
  not only to your interactive terminal.
- If you edited a configuration file, restart or reload the client and inspect its MCP server
  status or output.
- If a shared project configuration is pending, approve the workspace and the server after
  reviewing its command.
- If answers mix release lines, name either **stable** or **preview** explicitly in the prompt.

guides.title: Migrating from v1 to v2
guides.description: The breaking changes on the v2 line, in the order you will hit them, with the replacement for each.
guides.body:
v2 removes two long-deprecated APIs, moves the whole surface to `ValueTask`, and replaces
runtime assembly scanning with compile-time registration. This page lists what breaks and
what to do about it.

{% aside %}
v2 is the stable line. v1.x receives no further work, so this migration is the supported path
forward — everything below applies to a stable release, not to a moving preview.
{% /aside %}

## 1. `AmbientExecutionContext` is gone

Deprecated since v1.2.0, removed in v2. The dispatch path now carries **zero `AsyncLocal`
state**, which is what makes nested and parallel dispatch predictable.

```csharp
// v1
var tenant = AmbientExecutionContext.Current.Get<string>("tenant");

// v2 — the context is a parameter on every handler and interceptor
public ValueTask HandleAsync(DoThing command, IExecutionContext context)
{
    var tenant = context.Get<string>("tenant");
    …
}
```

If a helper deep in your call stack needed the ambient context, pass `IExecutionContext`
down to it, or read what it needs in the handler and pass that.

**`CreateScope` changed shape too.** It no longer takes a context to install:

```csharp
// v1
using (var _ = context.CreateScope(new ExecutionContext())) { … }

// v2 — returns a struct scope carrying a child context you pass explicitly
using var scope = context.CreateScope();
await _commands.SendAsync(new Inner(), scope.Context);
```

See [Nested dispatch](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch).

## 2. `Task` becomes `ValueTask`

Handlers, interceptors and the mediator facades all return `ValueTask` /
`ValueTask<TResult>`. Synchronously completing handlers now allocate nothing.

```csharp
// v1
public Task<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, IExecutionContext context)
    => Task.FromResult(Guid.NewGuid());

// v2
public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, IExecutionContext context)
    => ValueTask.FromResult(Guid.NewGuid());
```

Mechanical replacements:

| v1 | v2 |
|---|---|
| `Task` | `ValueTask` |
| `Task<T>` | `ValueTask<T>` |
| `Task.CompletedTask` | `ValueTask.CompletedTask` |
| `Task.FromResult(x)` | `ValueTask.FromResult(x)` |

{% aside type="caution" %}
`ValueTask` must not be awaited twice or stored for later. If you were caching a returned
`Task`, call `.AsTask()` on the `ValueTask` first.
{% /aside %}

## 3. Three-parameter `TModifiedResult` interceptors are gone

Deprecated in v1.4.0, removed in v2. The two-parameter typed interfaces now expose the typed
`HandleAsync` directly:

```csharp
// v1
public class Stamp : ICommandPostInterceptor<CreateProduct, Guid, Guid> { … }

// v2
public sealed class Stamp : ICommandPostInterceptor<CreateProduct, Guid>
{
    public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, Guid result, IExecutionContext context)
        => ValueTask.FromResult(result);
}
```

## 4. `RegisterFromAssembly` → `RegisterGenerated`

Still supported, but no longer the default path. Add the generator package and swap the call:

```bash
dotnet add package Stella.Ergosfare.SourceGenerator
```

```csharp
// v1
services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterFromAssembly(Assembly.GetExecutingAssembly())));

// v2
using Stella.Ergosfare.Generated;      // required — this is where the method lives

services.AddErgosfare(o => o
    .AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated()));
```

This is the change that gets you compile-time registration, reflection-free dispatch and a
clean Native AOT publish. Keep `RegisterFromAssembly` only for assemblies genuinely loaded at
runtime.

Watch for `ERGOSG001` / `ERGOSG002` after the switch: they flag types the generator found but
cannot name, which runtime scanning would have registered silently. See
[Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery#diagnostics).

{% aside type="caution" %}
This page describes the v1 → v2.0 move and is kept as written. Since then **v2.3 removed
`RegisterFromAssembly` entirely** — runtime assembly scanning is no longer supported at all,
so the "keep it for assemblies loaded at runtime" advice above no longer has an API behind it.
See [Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3](/ergosfare.docs/migration/v2.2-to-v2.3).
{% /aside %}

## 5. Event broadcast now matches handlers covariantly

In v1, only interceptors matched covariantly; event handlers had to name the exact event
type. In v2 a handler registered against a base type or interface receives every assignable
event.

```csharp
public sealed class AppendToOutbox : IEventHandler<IDomainEvent> { … }
```

**This can activate handlers that were previously dormant.** If you have an
`IEventHandler<IEvent>` or similar broad registration in a v1 codebase, it now runs for every
event. Narrow it, or opt individual messages out with
[`[ExcludeFromPipeline]`](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights).

## 6. Typed dispatch everywhere

Interceptor object roots and default-interface-method bridges were removed; invocation is
generic end to end. This affects you only if you implemented Ergosfare's internal
abstractions directly — normal handler and interceptor code is unaffected.

## What is new and worth adopting

Nothing here is required, but these are the reasons to be on v2 at all:

- [Compile-time discovery](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/compile-time-discovery), including
  cross-assembly registration with no code in the library.
- [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys) for registration-time
  feature gating.
- [Final interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/final-interceptors) — the stage
  that runs whether the pipeline succeeded or threw.
- [`[ExcludeFromPipeline]`](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/groups-and-weights) for
  keeping high-volume messages out of blanket interceptors.
- [Nested dispatch scopes](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch).
- [Native AOT support](/ergosfare.docs/advanced/aot-and-trimming) that actually holds under
  `PublishAot`.

## Suggested order

1. Add the source generator package, switch to `RegisterGenerated()`, fix `ERGOSG*` warnings.
2. Replace `Task` with `ValueTask` across handlers and interceptors — the compiler finds
   every site.
3. Remove `AmbientExecutionContext` usages; thread the execution context parameter instead.
   (It was `IExecutionContext` in v2.0–v2.2 and is `ErgosfareContext` from v2.3 on.)
4. Collapse three-parameter interceptors to their two-parameter form.
5. Audit broad `IEventHandler<…>` registrations for the new covariant delivery.
6. Then adopt what is new, at whatever pace suits you.

The full list of changes is in
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md); the
support policy is in
[COMPATIBILITY.md](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/blob/main/COMPATIBILITY.md).

guides.title: Migrating from v2.2 to v2.3
guides.description: What v2.3 removed, what replaced it, and the behaviour changes that compile cleanly but run differently.
guides.body:
v2.3 retires the runtime registry. The generator's **frozen composition table** is now the
authority for handler and interceptor relationships; registration selects from it, and
dispatch executes that selection without reflective scanning or runtime pipeline mutation.

Most of this migration is mechanical and the compiler finds it for you. Two changes are not:
`Abort` and the abort-time behaviour of the final stage compile cleanly and behave
differently. Read §5 even if everything else builds.

{% aside %}
This is a stable-to-stable move within the v2 line. The removals were staged: v2.2 marked the
assembly-scanning surface `[Obsolete]` one release ahead of removing it, so a project that
builds warning-free on v2.2 has most of the work already done.
{% /aside %}

## 1. `IMessageRegistry` and the descriptor surface are gone

Registration no longer *discovers* anything. The generator compiles every handler and
interceptor relationship in the closure into an immutable table before the application runs;
`RegisterGenerated()` and `Register<T>()` record which of its rows this container serves.

```csharp
// v2.2 — the module handed you a registry to feed
public void Build(IModuleConfiguration configuration)
{
    _builder(new CommandModuleBuilder(configuration.MessageRegistry));
    configuration.Services.TryAddScoped<ICommandMediator, CommandMediator>();
}

// v2.3 — the module hands you a catalog to select from
public void Build(IModuleConfiguration configuration)
{
    _builder(new CommandModuleBuilder(configuration.Compositions));
    configuration.Services.TryAddTransient<ICommandMediator, EngineBackedCommandMediator>();
}
```

`IModuleConfiguration` is now `{ IServiceCollection Services; FrozenCompositionCatalog Compositions; }`.

**What to do.** If you never wrote a custom `IModule`, nothing — the built-in modules carry
this themselves. If you did, swap `MessageRegistry` for `Compositions` and `Register…` for
`Select`. Selection is a union: repeated and overlapping calls stay harmless.

Removed with it: `IHandlerDescriptor` and the descriptor surfaces, `RegisterDescriptors(...)`,
and `IModuleBuilder`. The concrete builders remain, and their bulk path is now
`RegisterParticipants(IEnumerable<Type>)`.

## 2. `RegisterFromAssembly` is removed

Runtime assembly scanning is gone from every module builder. There is no replacement, because
there is nothing for it to do: an assembly loaded after compilation cannot append a message
shape to a frozen table.

`ResultAdapterBuilder` went with it. Result adapters now bind declaratively per message with
`[ResultAdapter]`, or application-wide through
`IModuleRegistry.UseDefaultResultAdapter(Type)` — both `[Experimental]` under `ERGOEXP001`.
See [Configuring](/ergosfare.docs/getting-started/configuring#result-adapters).

```csharp
// v2.2
.AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterFromAssembly(typeof(CreateProduct).Assembly))

// v2.3
.AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated())
```

**Selective registration keeps working** — it just happens at compile time. Tag the slice and
select it by pattern:

```csharp
[assembly: DiscoveryKey("payments")]          // in the slice's assembly

.AddCommandModule(c => c.RegisterGenerated("payments.*"))
```

See [Discovery keys](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/discovery-keys). For a plugin host, compile
the plugin contracts into the closure the generator sees and choose among them at registration
time; a genuinely late-loaded assembly is outside the model.

## 3. `IExecutionContext` → `ErgosfareContext`

The interface is replaced by a **public sealed class**. Every handler and interceptor contract
takes the concrete type, which removes an interface dispatch whose only implementation was
internal.

```csharp
// v2.2
public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, IExecutionContext context)

// v2.3
public ValueTask<Guid> HandleAsync(CreateProduct command, ErgosfareContext context)
```

A find-and-replace across handlers and interceptors covers it; the compiler finds anything
missed.

**New in exchange: a public constructor.** Both parameters are optional, so you can own a
context — for a test, or to hand one to an engine-level dispatch:

```csharp
using var cts = new CancellationTokenSource();
var context = new ErgosfareContext(cancellationToken: cts.Token);
```

A context you construct is never pooled, so the pooling lifetime rule does not apply to it.

## 4. `ExecutionContextScope` → `ErgosfareContextScope`

Renamed, and its constructor is now **internal**: `context.CreateScope()` is the only way to
get one. A scope always has a parent, which is what the type was always supposed to mean.

```csharp
// v2.2 and v2.3 alike — this was already the idiom
using var scope = context.CreateScope();
await _commands.SendAsync(new ReserveStock(id), scope.Context);
```

If you constructed a scope directly anywhere, that code has to go through `CreateScope()`.
Disposing a default scope remains a no-op.

## 5. `Abort` cuts the pipeline and reaches the caller

**This is the change that compiles cleanly and behaves differently.** Read it even if your
build is green.

```csharp
// v2.2 — seeded a result, ended the pipeline quietly, final interceptors still ran
context.Abort(Guid.Empty);

// v2.3 — throws ExecutionAbortedException; nothing downstream runs
context.Abort("not permitted to create products", _user.Id);
```

Three overloads: `Abort()`, `Abort(reason)`, `Abort(reason, value)`. There is no result
argument, whatever the message's result type — a cut pipeline produced none, and returning the
type's default was indistinguishable from a handler that legitimately produced nothing.

Three consequences to audit:

**The caller now sees it.** Wrap dispatches whose pipelines can abort:

```csharp
try
{
    var id = await commands.SendAsync<Guid>(new CreateProduct("Laptop", 999m));
}
catch (ExecutionAbortedException aborted)
{
    logger.LogInformation("refused: {Reason}", aborted.Reason);
    if (aborted.Value is Guid userId) { … }
}
```

**Final interceptors no longer run after an abort.** Nothing downstream does: not the rest of
the current stage, not the exception stage, not the final stage. Cleanup that must survive an
abort moves to the caller's own `try`/`finally`.

**Nested dispatch propagates by default.** An inner abort travels out of the inner call and,
unless the outer handler catches it, out of the outer pipeline too. Nested code written
against the old "inner abort ends only the inner pipeline" behaviour needs the `try` added
explicitly — see [Nested dispatch](/ergosfare.docs/core-concepts/nested-dispatch).

**Short-circuiting with a cached result is no longer an interceptor pattern.** Nothing before
the handler can supply the pipeline's result. Read the cache in the handler, or in a handler
that decorates the real one.

## 6. `AddCoreModule` and the core module are removed

`AddCoreModule`, `CoreModule`, `CoreModuleBuilder` and `IModuleBuilder` are gone. Plain
messages — anything that was neither command, query nor event — move to the **event module**,
which is the open lane:

```csharp
public interface IEventHandler<in TEvent> : IEvent, IAsyncHandler<TEvent>
    where TEvent : notnull;
```

`TEvent` is unconstrained beyond `notnull`, and `PublishAsync<TEvent>(TEvent)` matches it, so
a POCO — a plain class, a `record struct`, a wire contract you do not own — publishes as-is.

```csharp
// v2.2
services.AddErgosfare(o => o.AddCoreModule(m => m.Register<TelemetryPing>()));
await mediator.Mediate(new TelemetryPing(), options);

// v2.3
services.AddErgosfare(o => o.AddEventModule(e => e.RegisterGenerated()));
await events.PublishAsync(new TelemetryPing());
```

`ForceMemoizedHandlers()` is unaffected and still lives on `IModuleRegistry`.

## 7. Cross-cutting interceptors carry their markers

An interceptor written over the core contracts joins the built-in module partitions by
implementing their marker interfaces directly — the same idiom the module contracts use
(`ICommandPreInterceptor : ICommand, IAsyncPreInterceptor<ICommand>`):

```csharp
public sealed class LoggingInterceptor
    : IAsyncPreInterceptor<IMessage>, ICommand, IQuery, IEvent
{
    public ValueTask<object> HandleAsync(IMessage message, ErgosfareContext context) { … }
}
```

The generator takes it into all three partitions, and covariant matching gives it a row on
every message. `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` — blanket or group-scoped — drops it from the messages
that should not carry it.

## 8. `MediateOptions` and the low-level mediate surface are removed

`MediateOptions`, `ActualTypeOrFirstAssignableTypeMessageResolveStrategy`, the message-resolve
strategies and the low-level `IMessageMediator.Mediate` entry point are gone. The facades —
`SendAsync`, `QueryAsync`, `StreamAsync`, `PublishAsync` — are the dispatch surface, and they
are also the fast one: the options path ran its own resolve and mediation strategies and
reached neither the generated plans nor the straight-through path.

`IMessageMediator` itself remains, as the type-erased entry point for a message whose static
type the call site does not know:

```csharp
ValueTask         DispatchAsync(object message, ErgosfareContext context, IEnumerable<string>? groups = null);
ValueTask<TResult> DispatchAsync<TResult>(object message, ErgosfareContext context, IEnumerable<string>? groups = null);
```

`IPoolReturnable` is removed as well.

## 9. Behaviour that changed without an API change

| Change | What to audit |
|---|---|
| Resultless commands and events carry `Unit.Value` after successful execution | Post, exception and final interceptors that treated the result slot's `null` as "resultless". `null` now means "no result was produced". |
| A sole direct handler wins outright over any covariant candidates; two candidates **at the same level** raise `MultipleHandlerFoundException` before either runs | Messages with two handlers registered at the same level. The generator reports `ERGOSG010` at build time. |
| An exception is swallowed only when an interceptor that actually matched it returns a value | Nothing to change for untyped interceptors — they match everything, so they behave exactly as before. The rule matters once you adopt a typed `...For<TException>` contract: one whose filter does not match leaves the original exception and stack untouched. |
| `NoHandlerFoundException` derives from `InvalidOperationException` and exposes `MessageType`; missing and filtered-out handlers use it consistently | `catch` clauses ordered so a broader `InvalidOperationException` arm no longer shadows it. |
| A selected participant the container cannot resolve fails before the first stage with `UnresolvableParticipantException` | Participants selected but never registered with DI — previously a later, less obvious failure. |
| Event publication honours `ThrowIfNoHandlerFound` for every no-subscriber shape | Publishers that relied on a silent no-op for one of the shapes. |
| Mediator facades are registered transient rather than scoped | Code that resolved a facade once and cached it as scoped state. Handlers still resolve from the calling scope. |

{% aside type="tip" %}
**Nothing here asks you to rewrite your exception interceptors.** The untyped contracts —
`ICommandExceptionInterceptor<TCommand, TResult>` and its query and event equivalents — are
unchanged and not deprecated; they remain the right shape when one interceptor handles several
exception types, or logs every failure. The typed `...For<TException>` family added alongside
them is an option to adopt where it fits, one type at a time. See
[Exception interceptors](/ergosfare.docs/cross-cutting-concerns/exception-interceptors#declaring-the-exception-type).
{% /aside %}

## 10. Target frameworks

Packages now carry `net11.0` beside `net10.0` and `net9.0`. Nothing is required of you: a
`net11.0` project already bound `lib/net10.0/` through roll-forward, and no .NET 11 or C# 15
feature is adopted. Until .NET 11 reaches GA on 2026-11-10 the `net11.0` assets are compiled
against preview reference packs and will be re-packed against the GA pack.

Building *the repository* now needs the .NET 11 preview SDK. That affects contributors, not
consumers.

## Suggested order

1. Build on v2.2 and clear every `[Obsolete]` warning first — that is most of §1 and §2.
2. Rename `IExecutionContext` → `ErgosfareContext` and `ExecutionContextScope` →
   `ErgosfareContextScope`.
3. Swap remaining `RegisterFromAssembly` calls for `RegisterGenerated()`, adding discovery
   keys where the scan was selective.
4. Move `AddCoreModule` traffic to the event module.
5. **Audit every `Abort` call site and every nested dispatch** (§5). This is the step the
   compiler cannot do for you.
6. Audit the behaviour table in §9, then fix the `ERGOSG*` diagnostics the build reports.

The full list of changes is in
[CHANGELOG.md](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md); the
support policy is in
[COMPATIBILITY.md](https://github.com/stellayazilim/ergosfare/blob/main/COMPATIBILITY.md).

guides.title: Ergosfare
guides.description: A source-generated, high-performance mediator for CQRS-style messaging in .NET — commands, queries and events over one pipeline model.
guides.body:
import { Card, CardGrid } from '@astrojs/starlight/components'; import { StarField } from "../../../components/constellation/starfield.tsx"
A Roslyn generator discovers handlers in your compilation *and* in referenced assemblies, pre-computes their descriptors, and emits `AddGenerated()`. A library's handlers register with no registration code in the library. Generated dispatch roots close executor generics at compile time; pipeline plans pre-close generic handler types. No `MakeGenericType`, no registry scan, no `AsyncLocal` on the hot path. Pooled execution contexts and a `ValueTask`-first surface: 100k sequential dispatches allocate 2.3 MB, against MediatR's 18.3 MB for the same loop. `context.CreateScope()` gives a handler an isolated child context with inherited cancellation — the pattern ambient-state mediators cannot offer safely. Every construct referenced statically via `typeof`; dispatch roots anchor every generic instantiation, `record struct` messages included. Commands, Queries and Events are independent packages over a shared core. `IModule` is a real extension point — the shipped modules use it too.

guides.title: Native AOT and trimming
guides.description: Why compile-time dispatch makes NativeAOT viable, what still needs care, and how to check before you publish.
guides.body:
Ergosfare treats a published NativeAOT application as a first-class case. The reason is the same
compile-time work everything else rests on: if the shape of a dispatch is decided while you
compile, there is nothing left for it to construct reflectively.

## What makes it work

**No assembly scan.** Discovery happens at compile time, and `AddGenerated()` names every
construct through `typeof` — which is exactly what the trimming analyzers want to see.

**Generic instantiations are closed in generated code.** A dispatch would otherwise have to
close its executor generic with `MakeGenericType`, which only a JIT can answer. The generated
dispatch roots close them ahead of time, so the type the runtime needs already exists in the
published binary.

**Native result carriers name their own adapter.** Binding a result slot used to close an
adapter generic reflectively; the carrier now answers for itself, which removed the majority of
the adapter layer's reflective bindings along with their `IL2055` and `IL3050` suppressions.

**Nothing depends on a type's name.** No convention scanning, so the linker renaming or removing
things cannot break resolution.

## Publishing

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <PublishAot>true</PublishAot>
  <TrimMode>full</TrimMode>
</PropertyGroup>
```

```bash
dotnet publish -c Release -r linux-x64
```

## What still needs care

### Dispatching through a base type

```csharp
IMessage message = await queue.ReadAsync();
await mediator.DispatchAsync(message, ct);
```

The pipeline that runs belongs to the runtime type, which is correct — but the compiler now
cannot see which message arrives, so it cannot prove a root exists for it. If nothing in the
compilation ever names that message concretely, the dispatch falls back to closing its generic
at run time.

Turn on `ERGO009` to find these:

```ini
dotnet_diagnostic.ERGO009.severity = warning
```

Where the types *are* known, name them:

```csharp
var id = await mediator.SendAsync<PlaceOrder, Guid>(command, ct);
```

That is what the typed overloads are for — not throughput, but keeping the construction path off
reflection.

### Generic messages

A generic message's closed forms are not rooted, because an open definition is not a dispatchable
message. `Wrap<int>` and `Wrap<string>` are separate closed types, and the generator has no list
of which ones your application uses.

If you dispatch generic messages under AOT, root them yourself by dispatching each closed form
somewhere the compiler can see, or avoid generic messages on that path.

### Types hidden from discovery

`[ExcludeFromDiscovery]` keeps a type out of bulk registration. It does **not** stop it being
dispatched — and every hidden message your compilation declares is rooted anyway, precisely so a
hidden message does not become the shape that works in development and fails at publish.

Assembly-level exclusion is different: `[assembly: ExcludeFromDiscovery]` says do not look here
at all, and those types are neither registered nor rooted.

### Registrations naming a runtime type

`Register(someComputedType)` cannot be followed by any of this, which is why it is `ERGO018` —
an error rather than a warning.

### Your own code

The framework's dispatch path is reflection-free; your handlers are your own. JSON
serialization, `Activator.CreateInstance`, dynamic proxies and expression compilation all need
the same care they need in any AOT application.

## Checking before you ship

**Publish in CI, and run the binary.** This is the only check that actually proves anything.
Trimming warnings are useful, but the failure mode being avoided here — a generic that cannot be
closed — shows up when the code path executes.

**Exercise every dispatch shape in a smoke test.** A dispatch that is never executed is a
dispatch whose root you never confirmed.

**Read the trimming warnings.** `IL2026`, `IL2055`, `IL3050` from your own code are real; the
framework should contribute none.

## Trimming without AOT

`PublishTrimmed` alone gets most of the size benefit with fewer constraints, and is a good first
step if AOT is not a requirement:

```xml
<PublishTrimmed>true</PublishTrimmed>
```

The handler trim pairs well with it:

```xml
<ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>true</ErgosfareTrimUnusedHandlers>
```

A handler no dispatch in the closure reaches is then left out of the registration entirely —
reported as `ERGO008` so the exclusion is visible — and the linker can drop it. It only applies
to pure handler types; one that also carries interceptor contracts stays registered for those.

{% aside type="caution" %}
The trim is driven by the same reachability judgment as `ERGO007`, so it is only as good as the
compiler's view. A handler dispatched somewhere invisible — reflectively, or from an assembly
without a manifest — would be trimmed too. Suppress `ERGO007` at those types before turning the
trim on, and the exclusion respects the suppression.
{% /aside %}

## Known gaps

Two shapes still reach the reflective arm, and both are tracked:

- **Generic messages**, whose closed forms are never rooted.
- **A hidden message no registration names at all**, which nothing can enumerate.

Neither is a failure in a JIT run. Both are worth knowing about before an AOT publish.

guides.title: Experimental APIs
guides.description: Surfaces that are still moving, what "experimental" commits to, and how to opt in.
guides.body:
Three parts of the framework are marked experimental. They work, they are tested, and they ship —
what is not settled is their **shape**, and using one means accepting that it may change in a
minor release.

Each surface produces a warning with its own diagnostic ID. Suppression is optional unless your project treats warnings as errors. The markers use `Obsolete` with an experimental message and a custom `ERGOEXP` ID; IDEs may also display obsolete styling.

| Id | Surface |
|---|---|
| `ERGOEXP001` | the declarative result-adapter surface |
| `ERGOEXP002` | the plugin surface |
| `ERGOEXP003` | stream input and pipe converters |

## ERGOEXP001 — result adapters

`[ResultAdapter]`, `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, and `UseDefaultResultAdapter` with its carrier.

What the value channel *does* is settled: a failing pipeline can hand the caller a failed
carrier instead of throwing, and the exception interceptors still see the failure. How it is
*declared* is what may still move.

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .UseDefaultResultAdapter(typeof(ResultAdapter<>))
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

Opt in for the project:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP001</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## ERGOEXP002 — plugins

Everything in `Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions` — `[ErgosfarePlugin]`,
`[PipelineInvokable]`, `[PluginServiceFilter]`, the `Hook` and `Module` enums — together with the
module facade the generator emits from them.

For a **consumer**, the surface is one line, and that is where the suppression goes:

```csharp
#pragma warning disable ERGOEXP002
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddTiming()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
#pragma warning restore ERGOEXP002
```

For a **plugin author**, the whole package is built on it, so the project-wide form is more
practical:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP002</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

See [Plugins](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/plugins).

## ERGOEXP003 — stream input

`CommandStream<TChunk, TSelf>` and `QueryStream<TChunk, TSelf>` carry metadata as message
properties and input as a bounded, single-consumer asynchronous sequence. `Pipe` starts
production immediately; capacity limits queued items. The root `ErgosfareStream` implements
`IAsyncDisposable`. The explicit `IBufferWriter<T>` staging buffer grows separately, and
`FlushAsync` applies backpressure when publishing staged items.

Use `IPipeConverter<T>` for stateful conversion from a byte stream, and
`IPipeConverter<S,T>` or delegate overloads for per-item conversion. Byte blocks and
UTF-8 line helpers leave the source open. See the
[streaming multipart upload recipe](/ergosfare.docs/preview/recipes/streaming-upload).

Generated output-stream plans send failures directly to the consumer and final stage;
exception interceptors do not turn a failed stream into a replacement result. Early output
disposal reports `StreamOutputDisposedException` to pending input producers and final
interceptors. Explicit context abort still skips finals. Stream-specific post signatures
and cancellation supplied only through output `WithCancellation` remain design work;
pass the cancellation token to mediator dispatch and dispose unused inputs explicitly.

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <NoWarn>$(NoWarn);ERGOEXP003</NoWarn>
</PropertyGroup>
```

## What the marker commits to

**It will keep working in the release it shipped in.** Experimental is not unfinished — these
surfaces carry tests like everything else.

**It may change shape in a minor release.** An attribute may be renamed, a parameter added, an
enum member removed. The plugin surface has already been through this once: it had six
addressable stages, two of which let a plugin change a consumer's pipeline structure, and it
was cut back to four observation-only hooks.

**A change will be in the changelog with a migration note.** The two-parameter pre-interceptor
removal is the template — what went, why, and what replaces it.

## Where the line is

Something is experimental when *how you express it* is still being worked out. Once the
spelling has survived real use, the marker comes off and the surface joins the ordinary
compatibility promise.

The rest of the framework — the message contracts, the mediators, interceptors, discovery,
groups, weights — is not experimental and does not change shape in a minor release.

## Should you use them

**Result adapters:** yes, if your application already carries failures as values. It replaces
the try/catch you would write in every handler, and the declaration is the only part that might
move.

**Plugins:** yes for internal packages, where you control both sides and can update together.
For a package published to third parties, weigh it — your consumers inherit the suppression and
the churn.

Either way, pin the exact version. In a preview line a floating reference turns a shape change
into a surprise at restore time.

guides.title: Performance
guides.description: What a dispatch actually does at run time, which pipelines get a compiled plan, and what stops one from being built.
guides.body:
The performance story is a single idea: **do the shape work once, at compile time, and let a
dispatch be the work you asked for.** This page is about what that means concretely, and what
takes a pipeline off the fast path.

## What a dispatch does

For a message with a compiled plan:

1. Look the plan up — one dictionary hit, keyed by message type and group set.
2. Check the plan against the composition the container actually built.
3. Run the plan: a straight line of calls with the interceptors already in place.

There is no reflection, no `MakeGenericType`, no descriptor list to sort, no `AsyncLocal`, and
no context allocation — contexts are pooled and returned when the dispatch completes.

Handler and interceptor *instances* still come from the dispatching scope, because that is what
makes scoped dependencies work. For participants the generator can prove are plain transients
with a single public constructor, even that goes: the plan constructs them with `new`.

## What gets a plan

Three families, in order of how specific they are:

**Single-handler plans** — a message whose whole pipeline is one handler and no interceptors.
The cheapest possible shape.

**Staged plans** — a message with interceptors, emitted as a class whose body is the pipeline
written out. One per `(message, group set)`.

**Broadcast plans** — the same, for a publish that delivers to several subscribers.

Everything else takes the general path, which is correct and measurably slower.

## What stops a plan from being built

A plan is only built when the generator can settle every part of the pipeline. Any of these
leaves a message on the general path:

- A **keyed** participant, whose presence depends on which container was built.
- A **nested** participant type — the runtime orders segments by `Type.FullName`, whose nested
  separator sorts differently from the display name's dot.
- Several registrations reaching the same participant, whose order among its own appearances is
  not modelled.
- An **exception filter** that cannot be reproduced as an `is` test.
- A message declaring **several result contracts**, so the result is named at the call rather
  than by the message.
- `[ExcludeFromPipeline]` on the message.
- A **stream query** — the streaming lane has no plan family.

None of these is a defect. They are cases where the compiler declines to guess, and the general
path handles them correctly.

## The plan is always checked

Before running a plan, the executor compares the composition it was baked against with what the
container composed, segment by segment. A mismatch falls back.

This is what makes the whole mechanism safe rather than clever: a stale or wrong plan costs you
the speedup and never the behaviour.

## Groups and plans

A group set is part of what keys a plan, so a message dispatched under two constant sets gets
two plans — each a straight line with exactly the participants that set selects. Filtering does
not happen per dispatch.

A dispatch naming a set the compiler cannot read gets one plan carrying every participant, with
each one's membership evaluated at run time. Still a compiled plan; it just does the selection
you deferred.

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(command, GroupSet.Of("audit"));  // its own plan
await mediator.SendAsync(command, _configured);           // one filtering plan
```

A `static readonly GroupSet` is readable, so naming a set once and reusing it keeps the faster
shape.

## The typed dispatch overloads

Naming both types at a call site:

```csharp
var id = await mediator.SendAsync<PlaceOrder, Guid>(command, ct);
```

This is **not** a throughput optimisation — paired benchmark runs put the typed and untyped
lanes within a nanosecond of each other, in both directions. The untyped lane already answers
in a single dictionary lookup.

What it buys is the **construction path**: the executor closes from arguments the compiler
already resolved, so the arm that would otherwise reach `MakeGenericType` for a message with no
generated root is never taken. That is a NativeAOT concern, not a hot-path one.

## Memoized handlers

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry.ForceMemoizedHandlers());
```

Keeps resolved participants rather than resolving per dispatch. Worth it only when handlers are
genuinely stateless and their dependencies are singletons — a background worker draining a
queue. It is wrong anywhere a handler depends on something scoped, because the captured instance
outlives the scope that produced it.

## Where the remaining cost is

**Your handler.** Once the pipeline is a straight line, what is left is the work you wrote.

**Container resolution**, for participants that could not be proven directly constructible.
`ERGO003` tells you when several public constructors are the reason.

**Broad interceptors.** One written against `ICommand` runs for every command *and* every nested
dispatch. That is a design cost; narrowing the contract is the fix.

## Measuring it

The repository carries a BenchmarkDotNet suite covering each lane, including paired typed and
untyped runs so the claims above stay checkable rather than remembered.

For your own application, measure the dispatch against a direct method call on the same handler.
The gap is the framework's cost, and it should be small enough to be uninteresting next to
whatever the handler does.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Before optimising anything here, check whether your messages get plans at all. Dump the
generated file and look — a `StagedPlan` class for your message means the fast path is in play,
and its absence usually points at one of the reasons listed above.
{% /aside %}

guides.title: Plugins
guides.description: Shipping cross-cutting behaviour as a package — the four hooks, plugin options, and what a plugin deliberately cannot do.
guides.body:
A plugin is a NuGet package that observes pipelines. Install it, and its code runs at named
points inside every dispatch the consuming application makes — with no registration to write
and no interceptor to wire up.

{% aside type="caution" %}
The plugin surface is experimental and marked `ERGOEXP002`. Installing a plugin is the one line
of it you write yourself, and it is where the suppression goes. See
[Experimental APIs](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/experimental-apis).
{% /aside %}

## Installing one

```csharp
services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddTiming()
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

`AddTiming()` is generated into the plugin's own assembly, so the consumer calls an ordinary
extension method. If the plugin declares options, the call takes them:

```csharp
.AddTiming(new TimingOptions { Threshold = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(200) })
```

That is the whole consumer surface.

## Writing one

Two things make an assembly a plugin: an assembly attribute naming it, and at least one method
marked with a hook.

```csharp
using Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions;

[assembly: ErgosfarePlugin("Timing")]
```

The name becomes the generated `TimingModule` and the `AddTiming()` extension, so pick
something that reads well at a call site.

```csharp
public sealed class TimingService(ILogger<TimingService> logger)
{
    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.PreMain)]
    public void BeforeHandler<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
        => context.Set("startedAt", Stopwatch.GetTimestamp());

    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.PostMain)]
    public void AfterHandler<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
    {
        if (context.TryGet<long>("startedAt", out var started))
            logger.LogInformation("{Message} took {Elapsed}",
                typeof(TMessage).Name, Stopwatch.GetElapsedTime(started));
    }
}
```

The class is registered as a singleton by the generated module. Its constructor dependencies
are resolved from the container, so a plugin service takes ordinary dependencies.

## The four hooks

```
Start → pre* → PreMain → handler → PostMain → post* → Finish
```

| Hook | Where it runs |
|---|---|
| `Hook.Start` | at the very beginning of the dispatch |
| `Hook.PreMain` | after the pre-interceptors, before the handler |
| `Hook.PostMain` | after the handler, before the post-interceptors |
| `Hook.Finish` | at the end of a successful dispatch |

Every one of them is a **straight-line position that exists in every pipeline**. That is the
design constraint the whole surface is built around: no plan grows a `try`, a `catch` or a
`finally` because a plugin was installed. An interceptorless pipeline carrying calls at all four
hooks is still the straight line it is without them.

Points coincide rather than disappear. With no pre-interceptors, `Start` and `PreMain` name the
same instant and both calls run. In a broadcast, `PreMain` and `PostMain` name the seam around
a *delivery*, so they run once per subscriber.

## What a plugin cannot do

**It cannot see the failure path.** There is no hook on the exception or final stages, and this
is deliberate: those stages are what force a pipeline to carry a `try`/`finally`, and a
third-party package should not be able to change the shape of a consumer's pipeline by being
installed.

A plugin that genuinely needs the failure path ships an interceptor instead — a plugin package
can contain one like any other assembly, and the consumer's composition already knows how to
place it.

**It cannot change the message or the result.** A hook method returns `void` or `ValueTask`.
Hooks observe; interceptors participate.

## One signature, whatever the pipeline produces

A hook method takes one type parameter — its message — and nothing else varies:

```csharp
[PipelineInvokable(Hook.Start)]
public ValueTask OnStart<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context) { … }
```

No hook carries a result, so a void command, a result-producing query and an event broadcast
all call the same method the same way. A `void` method is called plainly and never enters the
state machine; a `ValueTask` one is awaited.

Parameters are filled positionally: the message from the dispatch, the `ErgosfareContext` from
the pipeline, and anything else resolved from the container.

## Narrowing where a hook runs

A generic constraint is how a plugin says which messages it applies to:

```csharp
[PipelineInvokable(Hook.PreMain)]
public void OnOrder<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
    where TMessage : IOrderMessage { … }
```

The call is closed over each plan's concrete types when it is written, so a constraint is both a
selection rule and something the emitted code has to satisfy. A constraint that cannot be
reproduced from type names — a constructed generic, `new()`, `unmanaged` — makes the whole
method unmodelable and it is passed over rather than guessed at.

`[PluginServiceFilter]` narrows by module family or discovery key:

```csharp
[PluginServiceFilter(Module.Command | Module.Query)]
public sealed class TimingService { … }
```

A method-level filter narrows the type's rather than replacing it: families intersect, and keys
add together.

## Plugin options

Name an options type in the assembly attribute:

```csharp
[assembly: ErgosfarePlugin("Timing", typeof(TimingOptions))]

public sealed class TimingOptions
{
    public TimeSpan Threshold { get; init; } = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100);
}
```

`AddTiming()` now takes an instance, and the module hands it to the service it constructs.

**The options never enter the container.** Nothing registers them, no resolution looks them up,
and the consumer constructs what they pass — so there is no builder in between and nothing
configurable the call site cannot see.

There are two ways for a service to receive them, chosen by what you write.

**Write a constructor.** It is left alone, and its other parameters are still resolved from the
container:

```csharp
public sealed class TimingService(TimingOptions options, ILogger<TimingService> logger) { … }
```

**Or make the class `partial` and write none.** The generator writes the field and the line that
assigns it:

```csharp
public sealed partial class TimingService
{
    [PipelineInvokable(Hook.Finish)]
    public void OnFinish<TMessage>(TMessage message, ErgosfareContext context)
        => _logger.LogInformation("threshold {T}", _options.Threshold);
}
```

A service that is neither — no constructor and not `partial`, or several public constructors —
is `ERGO017`, rather than silently ignoring settings its own plugin declared.

## Packaging

A plugin is an ordinary library that references `Stella.Ergosfare.Plugins.Abstractions` and the
source generator. The generator emits the module and the registry extension into the plugin's
own compilation, so nothing about this depends on one generator seeing another's output.

{% aside type="danger" %}
**Do not name a plugin assembly `Stella.Ergosfare.*`.** That prefix is reserved, and reference
scanning skips it — Ergosfare's own contract interfaces inherit the module markers and would
otherwise all register as user types. A plugin under the prefix would silently reach no
pipeline at all, so it is reported as `ERGO015`.

If you genuinely must live under the prefix, opt back in per assembly:

```csharp
[assembly: AssemblyMetadata("ErgosfareSourceGeneratorForceScanReferences", "true")]
```
{% /aside %}

## What it costs

Nothing while nothing is installed, and nothing structural when something is. A hook call is a
call at a point the pipeline already had. The plugin service is a singleton resolved once per
container, not per dispatch, and its per-dispatch dependencies arrive as method parameters —
which is why the lifetime is fixed rather than left to the author.

guides.title: Composition root and testing
guides.description: Where registration belongs, how to lay projects out so discovery works for you, and how to test a pipeline without mocking the mediator.
guides.body:
## One composition root

Register once, in the project that becomes your application. That is where the generator judges
reachability, because it is the only place that sees the whole closure — which is why `ERGO005`
and `ERGO007` appear when you build the executable rather than the library that declared the
handler.

```csharp
var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
    .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddQueryModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
    .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));
```

If your root is a library rather than an executable — a test host, a plugin container, a
function app — say so, or the judgments never run:

```xml
<PropertyGroup>
  <ErgosfareCompositionRoot>true</ErgosfareCompositionRoot>
</PropertyGroup>
```

Splitting registration across several places is the main way people lose the diagnostics.
Everything the compiler can tell you depends on one project seeing the whole picture.

## Laying projects out

A layout that works with discovery rather than against it:

```
MyApp.Domain            ← domain types, plain events. No Ergosfare reference.
MyApp.Application       ← messages, handlers, interceptors. Abstractions + generator.
MyApp.Infrastructure    ← implementations the handlers depend on.
MyApp.Api               ← composition root. Extensions + generator.
```

Three things make this work:

**Messages live with their handlers**, in the application layer. A message and the code that
serves it change together.

**Domain events stay plain.** A subscriber is what makes a type an event, so `MyApp.Domain` can
declare `OrderShipped` with no reference to anything.

**The generator is referenced in both the application layer and the root.** In the library it
finds handlers and records what that assembly dispatches; in the root it writes the registration
and runs the judgments.

## Libraries that ship handlers

A library's handlers register through the application that consumes it — the reference scan
finds them, and the library ships no registration code.

Two things to get right:

**Grant access to internal handlers**, or they are invisible to the consumer's generated code:

```csharp
[assembly: InternalsVisibleTo("MyApp.Api")]
```

Otherwise they surface as `ERGO002`. Making them `public` is the other answer.

**Give optional handlers a discovery key**, so a consumer opts in rather than getting them
whether they wanted them or not:

```csharp
[DiscoveryKey("myLibrary.optional")]
public sealed class OptionalHandler : ICommandHandler<Something> { … }
```

## Testing: build the real pipeline

The instinct to mock `ICommandMediator` is worth resisting. A mocked mediator tests that your
code called a mediator — it does not test that a handler exists, that its interceptors run, or
that the dispatch resolves at all. Those are exactly the things that break.

Build a container instead. It is a few lines, and it is the real thing:

```csharp
private static IServiceProvider BuildHost()
{
    var services = new ServiceCollection();

    services.AddSingleton<IOrderRepository, InMemoryOrderRepository>();
    services.AddErgosfare(registry => registry
        .AddCommandModule(module => module.AddGenerated())
        .AddEventModule(module => module.AddGenerated()));

    return services.BuildServiceProvider();
}

[Fact]
public async Task PlacingAnOrder_ReturnsItsId()
{
    using var scope = BuildHost().CreateScope();
    var mediator = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ICommandMediator>();

    var id = await mediator.SendAsync(new PlaceOrder(customerId, lines));

    Assert.NotEqual(Guid.Empty, id);
}
```

This runs the pipeline your application runs: the same handler selection, the same interceptors,
the same order.

{% aside type="tip" %}
Mark the test project a composition root. Then the reachability diagnostics run over your test
assembly too, and a test dispatching a message with no handler fails at build rather than at
run time.
{% /aside %}

## Testing a handler on its own

A handler is an ordinary class, so when you want to test its logic and nothing else, construct
it:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task Handler_SavesTheOrder()
{
    var repository = new InMemoryOrderRepository();
    var handler = new PlaceOrderHandler(repository, new FlatPricing());

    var id = await handler.HandleAsync(new PlaceOrder(customerId, lines),
                                       new ErgosfareContext());

    Assert.Single(repository.Saved);
}
```

Use both kinds. The unit test pins the logic; the container test pins that the logic is
reachable.

## Testing an interceptor

Through the pipeline, because ordering and matching are the parts worth testing. Register a
handler that records what it saw, dispatch, and assert on the effect:

```csharp
[Fact]
public async Task PreInterceptor_TrimsTheName()
{
    using var scope = BuildHost().CreateScope();
    var mediator = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<ICommandMediator>();
    var spy = scope.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<RecordingRepository>();

    await mediator.SendAsync(new CreateProduct("  Bench  ", 10m));

    Assert.Equal("Bench", spy.Last.Name);
}
```

Testing an interceptor by calling `HandleAsync` directly tells you the body works. It does not
tell you the interceptor is reached, which is usually the failure you are guarding against.

## Isolating tests from each other

Handler instances come from the dispatching scope, so a scope per test gives each one its own
scoped services:

```csharp
using var scope = provider.CreateScope();
```

Avoid `ForceMemoizedHandlers()` in tests unless you are specifically testing it. It keeps
resolved participants, which is exactly the state leak you do not want between cases.

## Before you ship

**Build the composition root with warnings as errors.** That is where the reachability
judgments run, and where `ERGO007` catches the handler whose dispatch you removed last week.

**If you publish NativeAOT, publish it in CI.** The compile-time work is what makes AOT viable,
but the way to know is to publish and run — see
[Native AOT and trimming](/ergosfare.docs/preview/advanced/aot-and-trimming).

guides.title: Working with diagnostics
guides.description: Every ERGO code, what it is telling you, and when suppressing one is the right answer.
guides.body:
Ergosfare's diagnostics are not style advice. Most of them report something that will go wrong
at run time, proved at compile time — so the default posture is to fix them, and suppressing
one should be a decision you can explain.

They come in two families: `ERGO###` for what the generator can prove about your code, and
`ERGOEXP###` marking a surface that is still moving.

## The errors

These fail the build, because each one describes a call that cannot work.

### ERGO005 — this dispatch can never reach a handler

Neither the dispatched type nor any subtype in the compiled closure has a handler.

```csharp
await mediator.SendAsync(new ArchiveOrder(id));   // nothing handles ArchiveOrder
```

**Fix:** write the handler, or delete the dispatch. It applies to publishing too — an event no
subscriber serves is a dead dispatch, and writing the event while forgetting the subscriber is
the ordinary way to get there.

**Legitimately suppress it** when the handler is registered somewhere the compiler cannot see:
a plugin container loading assemblies at run time, a test host registering by hand. Suppress at
the call site with a reason.

### ERGO010 — two handlers claim one message

A command or query has exactly one handler, and the priority ladder has no tiebreaker within a
level.

**Fix:** delete one; make one direct so it wins outright; or separate them by group or
discovery key if they are genuinely alternatives.

### ERGO011 / ERGO012 — result adapter annotations

`ERGO011` is a `[ResultAdapter]` naming an adapter that can never bind — it does not implement
the contract for any slot the message dispatches, or cannot be instantiated. `ERGO012` is a
message carrying both `[ResultAdapter]` and `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, which asks for two
opposite things.

### ERGO013 — a result no adapter serves

You configured a default result adapter, which makes value-carried failure the application's
contract — and this message's result cannot take part, so its pipeline keeps throwing.

**Fix:** return a carrier the adapter serves, declare a `[ResultAdapter]` for the message, or
acknowledge it with `[IgnoreResultAdapter]`, which turns it into the `ERGO014` warning instead.

### ERGO018 — a registration naming a runtime type

```csharp
registry.Register(typeof(T).Assembly.GetTypes().First());   // ERGO018
```

The closed world compiles a construct's pipeline, freezes its composition and bakes its plan
from what the compilation can see. A type known only at run time enters none of that, so the
registration cannot mean what it appears to.

**Fix:** `Register<T>()` or `Register(typeof(T))` with a concrete type, or let
`AddGenerated()` collect it.

## The warnings

### ERGO001 / ERGO002 — a type that cannot be named

`ERGO001` is a `private`, `protected` or file-local type in your own code. `ERGO002` is an
`internal` type in a referenced assembly with no `InternalsVisibleTo` grant for you.

**Fix:** make it `internal` at least, or grant access. Both say the declaration promises
something its accessibility takes back.

### ERGO006 — only subtypes are handled

The dispatched static type is a concrete message with no handler, while a subtype has one. An
instance of exactly that type throws.

**Fix:** usually the base type should be `abstract`. If instances of it are real, it needs its
own handler.

### ERGO007 — a handler nothing can reach

No dispatch in the compiled closure can deliver this handler's message.
